summary: Automated valuation is the sector's oldest deployed AI, and it is now formally regulated: federal quality-control standards for AVMs took effect in 2025. Valuation, leasing automation, 3D capture, and property operations are where AI actually runs; the regulator record and the platforms' own model documentation are the sources.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 28.0% of firms in real estate and rental and leasing reported using AI in the most recent period, up from 25.6% in the prior period, making it one of the more measurably active sectors in the survey. That figure covers the broad NAICS 53 category and reflects self-reported use over a two-week window, so it is a floor rather than a ceiling on actual deployment.

The oldest and most pervasive form of AI in the sector is the automated valuation model. Zillow publishes Zestimate valuations for more than 110 million homes using a neural network architecture that draws on county and tax assessor records, MLS feeds, listing signals, and historical sales data, with Zestimates updated multiple times per week. HouseCanary covers more than 136 million U.S. properties with AI-powered valuations and forecasts, combining machine learning with image recognition that identifies room types and assesses home condition directly from photos. Opendoor has deployed pricing models to serve over 307,535 homeowners through its instant-offer platform, a model that places real balance-sheet exposure behind the algorithm's output. On the commercial side, Prophia uses AI to extract key lease terms from documents and combines that extraction with expert validation to produce structured lease data, one of the clearest production uses of document AI in the sector.

Enterprise and commercial operators are automating building operations and tenant workflows. Building Engines, a JLL company, offers a platform called Prism that delivers AI-driven answers, recommendations, and automation for commercial property teams with the stated aim of cutting costs and growing net operating income. EliseAI provides an agentic conversational AI platform that handles messages, calls, tour scheduling, prospect follow-up, and maintenance requests around the clock for housing operators, positioning automation as a way to reduce overhead and free staff for higher-value tasks. Matterport digitizes physical buildings into 3D models with AI-assisted capture, enabling remote portfolio management and integration with construction platforms such as Procore and Autodesk. JLL states it has invested more in AI technology than any other real estate company, framing that spending as unlocking the potential of buildings and people across brokerage, facilities, and portfolio analytics.

The regulatory posture for the sector's most consequential AI, property valuation used in mortgage decisions, is now settled federal law. The CFPB, FHFA, OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and NCUA jointly adopted a final rule under the Dodd-Frank Act requiring mortgage originators and secondary market issuers that use automated valuation models to maintain quality control standards ensuring high confidence in AVM estimates, protection against data manipulation, avoidance of conflicts of interest, and random sample testing and reviews. Both the CFPB and FHFA publish the rule and its compliance requirements, and the CFPB's supervisory work on algorithmic appraisal extends to valuation bias and model accountability. These are the first binding federal rules specifically targeting AI in real estate, and any firm using AVMs in covered credit or securitization decisions must now have documented policies and control systems in place.

The venture and conference infrastructure around proptech is active. CREtech describes its New York conference as bringing together 3,000 leaders and facilitating more than 20,000 pre-scheduled one-on-one meetings, with sessions led by operators actively deploying AI across portfolios. The Center for Real Estate Technology and Innovation maintains a network of over 500 investors focused on real estate technology. NAR REACH, created by Second Century Ventures and described as the most active venture fund in the global real estate technology space, operates a zero-equity accelerator for residential proptech companies. BOMA International serves as the commercial sector's trade and advocacy body, tracking trends across building types including operations technology.

A reader evaluating deployment should note that the regulatory framework for valuation AI is now specific and enforceable, so compliance infrastructure is not optional for mortgage-adjacent uses. The document AI and leasing automation use cases, illustrated by Prophia and EliseAI, are relatively contained in scope and carry lower regulatory exposure, making them practical starting points. Valuation platforms such as HouseCanary are explicit that their AI combines machine learning with manual quality control, which reflects both the regulatory environment and the accuracy demands of institutional underwriting. The sector is well past early experimentation in several sub-verticals, but the Census figure of 28.0% also means that roughly seven in ten firms in the broad category have not yet reported active AI use, leaving substantial room for adoption to deepen.
